context: Real 90-minute NIH Clinical Center IPPCR 2015 lecture, 'Conceptual Approach to Survival Analysis', by Dr. Laura Lee Johnson of the US FDA, from human-authored captions with no speaker diarization. It covers time-to-event vocabulary, censoring and truncation, survival and hazard functions, Kaplan-Meier, the log-rank test and Cox proportional hazards models, illustrated with trial examples (zidovudine HIV transmission, liver cirrhosis) and ends with conclusions and course logistics.

facts.statement: Survival analysis is also called time-to-event analysis; the event need not be death and can be many other things.

The material is not going to make or break students on the exam; the goal is to understand the ideas well enough to read manuscripts/protocols, sit on an IRB, and know when to consult a specialist statistician.
Learning objectives: interpret a Kaplan-Meier graph, interpret Cox model covariates, and understand the basic assumptions and what goes wrong when they are not met.
Mother-infant HIV transmission trial (worked out by Dennis Dixon): zidovudine versus placebo, powered to detect a 33% reduction in transmission, from 30% to 20%.
facts.notes: captions read '33% transmission rate'; 30% to 20% is a one-third reduction

facts.statement: Sample sizes for time-to-event studies are driven by the number of events, so you have to back into the total sample size and also account for dropouts and loss to follow-up.
The trial's DSMB met twice a year; it used a group sequential design with a preplanned interim efficacy review, the first in February 1994, including mothers enrolled up to December 1993.

At the first interim analysis the DSMB looked at Kaplan-Meier curves of probability of transmission (y-axis 0-40%) versus weeks (x-axis), with a log-rank p value and numbers at risk per arm shown below.
At the first interim analysis the zidovudine arm showed an 8.3% transmission rate with a tight confidence interval, far lower than the expected 20%.

The DSMB recommended stopping the zidovudine trial after careful review of toxicity and transmission rates; zidovudine was provided to the control group and the US Public Health Service (and other countries) modified national guidelines.
Censoring lets you use partial follow-up information: e.g. an infant followed only to 24 weeks who has not seroconverted still contributes to the analysis.
Defining a time-to-event outcome requires an event definition, a time origin, a time scale, and the time at which the event occurs.
Event times may be interval-measured (e.g. negative at 12 weeks, positive at 24 weeks) or measured more continuously (e.g. exact date of death).
Kaplan-Meier is a simple estimator of survival that can be computed by hand (on a napkin) and can be stratified, e.g. by study arm or sex.

A competing risk is an event that removes a subject from risk of the event of interest (e.g. an infant dying of another infection before it could seroconvert; if you die of cancer you cannot die of a heart attack), and Kaplan-Meier has no sensible interpretation under competing risks.

Kaplan-Meier cannot handle covariates (only stratification), and with many stratification factors each curve may have only 3 or 4 people, too few for a robust curve; the Cox model is richer and takes continuous and multiple variables.

Survival analysis is used whenever the question is about events and when they happen: death, infections (possibly recurrent), myocardial infarction, hospitalizations, cancer recurrence; some events may never occur.

Engineers use the same methods under the name failure analysis (light bulbs, computer crashes); the balloon example measures 'time' as milliliters of air until bursting, and quality control uses these measures too.
The Kaplan-Meier paper was originally about a page and a half; two authors from different disciplines submitted essentially the same paper to JASA and the editor told them to combine into one paper.
A logistic regression at a fixed time (e.g. yes/no at five years) can be done but loses the information gained from censoring.
Flu example: if one drug resolves symptoms in 3 days and another in 7, measuring at 10 days (or even 7) makes them look the same; frequent measurement in survival analysis picks up those nuances.
Cox-2 inhibitors: short-term studies showed no excess deaths, but the hazard functions crossed, and a problem starting around 12-18 months was missed.
Survival analysis makes inference about event rates: the rate at time t among those still at risk at time t.
Report median survival (the time by which 50% of subjects have had the event), not mean survival; mean survival requires every subject to have had the event, so reporting mean survival is a red flag.
The basic survival (Cox-type) model is a baseline hazard multiplied by the exponential of a linear combination of covariates, which are often called prognostic factors.
Notation: lower-case t is the time axis with t=0 the time origin; capital T is the random variable for the time the event occurs.
The survival function S(t) is the probability that the event time T is greater than or equal to t, i.e. the proportion of the population still without the event by time t.
Typical time origins: diagnosis or start of treatment in clinical trials; first exposure in occupational epidemiology; birth in studies of lifespan.
Pancreatic cancer example (event death, origin surgery, scale months): survival at 9 months was about 25%, i.e. 9-month post-resection survival is 25%.
A survival curve is monotonically decreasing: it goes down or stays flat, never back up (it can also be plotted inverted as proportion with the event).
S(t)=0.3 at t=60 months means five-year survival probability is 30%, equivalently 70% of patients die within five years; with patients, say 'five-year survival is 30%'.
The hazard function (incidence rate, 'force of mortality') is the instantaneous event rate at time t and underlies all of survival analysis.
Hazards are usually not constant over time (e.g. after a myocardial infarction, surviving the first 30 days makes longer-term survival much better).
Hazard example: lambda(t)=1% at t=12 months means at one year patients are dying at 1% per month; at a year and a half the chance of dying in the following month might be 2%.
Time scale matters for hazards: 120,000 deaths per year is similar to 10,000 per month, 2,500 per week, or 357 per day, so the time increment must be defined.

Herpes study: event was recurrence of lesions after a primary episode; time origin (end of primary episode) was hard to define and needed agreement among doctors and patients at home; time scale was months from end of primary episode.
Nickel refinery study: event death from lung cancer, origin estimated as start of employment at the refinery (acceptable since lung cancer takes decades), scale years since first exposure.
Unique features of survival analysis: an event, progression along a dimension (usually time), variable length of progression, and the event may not happen while you are watching.
Sample size is based on the expected number of events, so studies (e.g. cardiovascular) enroll high-risk people to get enough events; covariates and case mix must be considered.
Truncation concerns entry into a study; right truncation means sampling only people who had the event (e.g. from a cancer registry), which leads to an underestimate of the survival function.
Left truncation (e.g. enrolling only people 65 or older, as in the Cardiovascular Health Study) means short survivors who died earlier are never observed.
Right censoring: subjects who have not had the event by the end of follow-up (e.g. study closes at 5 years) are censored; we know they had not had the event up to that point.

Left censoring: the event occurred before observation began, e.g. a 12-year-old who already smokes regularly when first interviewed about age of starting smoking, or children already infected with cytomegalovirus at enrollment.
Kaplan-Meier (and essentially all methods) handle right censoring fine; left censoring is not as easy.

The key assumption of survival analysis is independent censoring (and truncation independent of the outcome): subjects at risk at any time point are a random sample of the population at risk at that time.
Without independent censoring the hazard function estimate is biased and the survival analyses are worthless.

Withdrawal must be unrelated to subsequent risk; even accidental death may not be independent (e.g. a therapy that impairs balance), and moving away is not automatically independent censoring (people move for last-ditch therapies).
Investigators should keep tracking subjects who stop treatment or visits, at least checking whether they are alive or had the event.
In survival plots, solid symbols usually mark events and open circles (or hash marks) mark censored observations.

Type I censoring: everyone followed for the same time; type II censoring: observation stops after a set number of events (engineering, e.g. light bulbs); random censoring (more general) is what happens in clinical studies with staggered enrollment.
Software may expect a failure indicator (delta) or a censoring indicator, which are exact opposites, so check which one your software uses; T* denotes observed time (event or follow-up time).
Censoring can depend on a covariate (e.g. age, severity) and still be independent given that covariate if the covariate is in the model, e.g. a Cox model; censoring may differ between study arms.
If older subjects are enrolled only later in a trial, they have less possible follow-up; conditioning on age gives independent censoring given age, otherwise estimates are biased.
With competing risks, the relevant hazard is the risk of the event (e.g. cancer) among those still at risk of it; people who died of a heart attack are no longer at risk of cancer.
Fictitious polar bear plunge example (from her friend Craig): 3% die from the plunge each year, other-cause annual death rate is 2% for males and 1% for females, followed for ten years.
facts.notes: all numbers made up for illustration (line 493)

facts.statement: After ten years 25% of women vs 24% of men died from the plunge, prompting a misleading 'plunge kills women' headline; the difference arises because 33.5% of women vs 40% of men died of other causes, leaving more women at risk.
People always die of something, which precludes other events, so you must think about what else precludes the event of interest when interpreting event rates.
Kaplan-Meier estimate is a product of conditional probabilities: S(t) = previous S times (1 - events at t / number at risk at t), starting at S(0)=1.
Worked KM example: 20 at risk; at t=5, 2 events gives 1-2/20 = 0.9; at t=6, 18 at risk, no events, stays 0.9; at t=10, 15 at risk (3 censored between 6 and 10), 1 event gives 0.84.
facts.notes: captions say '20%' at risk at line 524; means 20 people

facts.statement: Worked KM example final step: at 13 months, risk set 14, 2 events, 1 - 2/14 times previous survival, stated as .42.
facts.notes: transcript states .42; from the stated numbers .84 x (1-2/14) = .72 (likely caption/slide error)

facts.statement: Censored subjects contribute to the risk set until they leave the study and are then removed from it.
If high-risk subjects enter the study early or late, the Kaplan-Meier curve will be biased (e.g. coming down faster than it should).
Comparing two KM curves with a z-test at a single time point requires choosing t arbitrarily and does not use all the data.
Kaplan-Meier-based analyses cannot handle time-dependent covariates, recurrent events, or competing risks.

The log-rank test compares event rates over all time points by comparing observed to expected numbers of events; it accounts for censoring and truncation but not covariates, time-dependent covariates, or recurrent events.
Log-rank results are biased under confounding or when prognostic factors are imbalanced between groups; a log-rank test gives only a p value with no measure of the size of the difference.
A stratified log-rank test compares within strata but loses power because each test uses a smaller sample, and continuous prognostic factors are hard to stratify.
KM plus log-rank may be enough in many randomized studies, but if that is all you get and other things go wrong, ask for more, such as Cox models.
Kaplan-Meier dates from the 1940s and early Cox models from the '70s; methods evolved as medicine improved (e.g. recurrences), mirroring the history of medicine.
When using the Cox proportional hazards model you must test the proportionality assumption.
In the Cox model a coefficient beta=0 corresponds to a hazard ratio of 1 (no difference in survival experience), and exp(beta) is the relative rate/risk associated with that prognostic factor.

The Cox model is semiparametric (baseline hazard unspecified) and multiplicative: a covariate multiplies the hazard rate by some factor, and proportional hazards requires that relative rate to be constant over time.
The general Cox model allows time-dependent covariates (e.g. repeated weights, medication changes) and stratification, but needs enough data (not 16 covariates with 20 people).

To test proportional hazards, fit a second model adding covariate x log(time) interactions and compare using a Wald test or partial likelihood ratio test; Schoenfeld residual plots are another option.
In one example, the likelihood ratio test for the two log-time interaction terms (2 degrees of freedom) gave p = .94, so proportional hazards could be assumed.

In a second example the partial likelihood ratio test gave p = .003, so proportional hazards failed; the drug x time interaction was significant (the drug's effect changed over time), not age, suggesting crossing hazards.
Stanford heart transplant study: early analyses failed to account for time to transplant, which had to be separated from time to death.

Take-home: Kaplan-Meier is simple but potentially misleading; Cox proportional hazards is the modern workhorse but must be checked for proportionality and more general Cox models may be needed; how and when time is measured matters.
Changes in protocol, especially inclusion/exclusion criteria or recruitment, must be accounted for in the analysis or the model can be badly misinterpreted.
Liver cirrhosis RCT (new treatment vs placebo; papers in The Lancet 1981, papers in '85, and a 2009 Cochrane review): one study reported a 2-year Kaplan-Meier survival probability of .88.

In the cirrhosis Cox model the treatment covariate (treatment=1, placebo=0) had coefficient -0.135, so the relative rate for a treated subject is exp(-0.135); other covariates were ascites (presence/absence) and prothrombin time (continuous).
facts.notes: prothrombin/ascites coefficients (1.773, .346) are garbled in captions

facts.statement: In the cirrhosis trial physicians initially avoided enrolling patients with ascites (sicker, toxicity concerns) until about a year and a half in, so KM censoring was not independent: the hazard was biased too small and the survival estimate too large.
Including ascites as a covariate in a Cox model restores independent censoring (with respect to ascites), so the coefficients and relative risks are correct.

Cox regression is the most robust general method because it keeps being extended; it provides a framework for inference about covariates, though you must have measured the right covariates and its assumptions are hard (but often doable) to test.
Survival analysis handles right censoring and left truncation, but not every form handles recurrent events and competing risks, which need fancier models.

Above all, analysis follows the design: clinical questions generate hypotheses, studies are designed to test them, and if an analysis does not answer the question or match the protocol you need a different analysis.
Post questions to the discussion board, which stays open about 2 weeks after the lecture; online viewers must use the separate board for this faculty member.
Students are asked to fill out course evaluations and send in examples; the lecturer returns in mid December for a summary, with several other lectures in between.

not_decisions.statement: Using logistic regression on a yes/no outcome at a fixed time instead of survival analysis (possible but loses information; not the focus of the lecture)
Oversampling older subjects later in the study to fix the risk set (a past student's suggestion; lecturer says it is easier to put age in the model)
Schoenfeld residual plots for testing proportional hazards (mentioned but explicitly not covered)
Methods for repeated/recurrent events (explicitly not covered)

distractors.statement: Joke that one of the best times to get medical care is in a clinical trial, and an anecdote about a study requiring patients within 6 months of death who were still alive 18-24 months later
Joke that some parents think if they wait long enough their child will get married; soccer goals taking a long time
Lecturer notes she has promised herself to fix a bracket on her slide every time she gives the lecture
Aside that the lecturer grew up somewhere warm so polar bear plunges strike her as nuts, and Lake Michigan is bitterly cold in January
The old belief that subjects moving out of the area is independent censoring
A past student's assumption that following everybody for one year makes censoring OK

summary_must_include: survival/time-to-event analysis = inference on event rates among those at risk; event, origin, scale must be defined (F22, F11)
survival function S(t)=P(T>=t) and hazard = instantaneous event rate, with worked examples (F26, F31, F30)
right vs left censoring and truncation (F41, F42, F39, F40)
independent censoring is the key assumption; violation biases hazard and makes analyses worthless (F44, F45)
Kaplan-Meier: product of conditional probabilities, handles right censoring, no covariates/competing risks/recurrent events (F57, F63, F14)
log-rank test: all time points, observed vs expected, p value only, biased by confounding/imbalance (F64, F65)
Cox PH model: semiparametric, exp(beta)=relative rate, beta=0 -> HR 1, must test proportionality (log-time interaction, p=.94 vs p=.003) (F70, F71, F69, F73)
zidovudine HIV trial: 8.3% transmission at interim, trial stopped, guidelines changed (F08, F09)
cirrhosis/ascites example: delayed enrollment of sicker patients biased KM survival too high; Cox with ascites fixes it (F81, F82)
conclusions: Cox most robust; analysis follows the design (F83, F85)
